claims.text: A DeepMD-type potential can be trained on representative high-temperature ab initio liquid configurations of a target multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
Replacing TOR-TILD's standard EAM reference with the trained deep-learning potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
The improved phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to standard EAM references.
The proposed intervention applies to refractory- or transition-metal-based multicomponent high-entropy alloys near 0.9–1.0 T_m.
High-temperature high-entropy-alloy liquids exhibit a large diversity of atomic configurations.
A DeepMD potential provides a many-body representation of atomic interactions.
The many-body representation improves sampling of the liquid configurational landscape.
Learning complex many-body interactions allows the potential to capture the full configurational diversity of the ab initio liquid.
A deep-neural-network potential can describe structural behavior in both solid and liquid high-entropy materials at melting temperatures.
Conventional EAM models oversimplify the relevant atomic interactions and inadequately represent the many configurations of the ab initio liquid.
TOR-TILD calculations using standard EAM potentials exhibit significant thermodynamic-integration mismatch.
Thermodynamic integration using the machine-learning potential will produce free-energy differences within 1–2% of full ab initio values.
Performance at lower temperatures or for extremely atypical alloy compositions may not show the proposed improvement.
The estimated 30–50% mismatch reduction is based on evidence from elemental and binary calculations.
The exact magnitude of improvement in complex multicomponent systems remains uncertain.
The hypothesis can be tested by parallel EAM- and DeepMD-referenced thermodynamic-integration calculations using identical simulation setups and a full ab initio free-energy benchmark.
Failure to obtain both at least a 30% mismatch reduction and agreement within 1–2% of the full ab initio free energy would falsify the hypothesis.
